title: Retaliation Summary Judgment Appeal
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia
proceduralPosture: District court granted summary judgment for employer on causation and pretext.
issuesPresented: Whether temporal proximity and comparator evidence created a genuine dispute.
Whether the district court applied the correct summary judgment standard.
Whether evidentiary objections preserved below limit the appellate record.
meritsRecord: Employee reported compliance irregularities and was terminated six weeks later.
Employer cited a reduction in force and documented performance concerns.
Two comparator employees were retained despite similar audit findings.
The district court excluded a late-filed declaration in a footnote.
The summary judgment order treated the timing evidence as weak but did not address one comparator memorandum.

issues.label: Comparator evidence at summary judgment
preservationFacts: The comparator argument was raised in opposition to summary judgment.
The district court resolved the comparator evidence in its summary judgment order.
recordSupportFacts: Two retained employees had similar audit findings.
The relevant personnel memoranda are available for appendix inclusion.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: Temporal proximity and comparator treatment created a genuine dispute of pretext.
The district court weighed inferences instead of crediting the nonmovant.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The comparators were not similarly situated in all relevant respects.
The reduction-in-force record independently supports summary judgment.

issues.label: Application of the summary judgment standard
preservationFacts: The summary judgment standard was central to the district court ruling.
recordSupportFacts: The order describes the standard and evaluates causation and pretext.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The court drew factual inferences in favor of the movant.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The court recited and applied the correct standard.

issues.label: Late evidentiary objection and excluded declaration
issues.standardOfReview: abuse of discretion or forfeiture-sensitive review
preservationFacts: The objection was raised late and addressed only in a footnote.
recordSupportFacts: The excluded declaration is absent unless the appendix includes the relevant record excerpt.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The declaration explained disputed timing and motive evidence.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The argument was forfeited or harmless because other evidence supported judgment.

title: Rule 54(b) Finality Trap Contract Appeal
shortCaption: HarborTech Supply LLC v. Piedmont Components, Inc.
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina
proceduralPosture: District court entered partial summary judgment on the main contract claim while counterclaims and fee issues remained pending, with no separate Rule 54(b) certification.
issuesPresented: Whether the partial judgment is final and appealable.
Whether unresolved counterclaims defeat appellate jurisdiction.
Whether pendent issues may be reviewed if jurisdiction is cured.
meritsRecord: The district court granted summary judgment for Piedmont on liability under a supply agreement.
HarborTech's fraud counterclaim and fee request remained unresolved.
No separate judgment or Rule 54(b) certification appears on the docket.
The notice of appeal identifies only the partial summary judgment order.
The parties disagree whether the counterclaims are factually intertwined with the contract ruling.

issues.label: Finality without Rule 54(b) certification
preservationFacts: Finality is reviewed independently by the court of appeals.
The notice of appeal references an order that did not dispose of every claim.
recordSupportFacts: The docket sheet shows pending counterclaims.
The partial judgment order lacks certification language.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The resolved claim is separable and effectively final.
The court should hold the appeal in abeyance if the district court can certify the judgment.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The appeal should be dismissed because unresolved counterclaims remain.
No Rule 54(b) certification or final judgment supports jurisdiction.

issues.label: Effect of unresolved counterclaims
preservationFacts: The counterclaims were pleaded and remain active on the district court docket.
recordSupportFacts: The amended answer and docket report identify fraud and fee counterclaims.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The remaining counterclaims do not alter the practical finality of the resolved contract claim.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The remaining claims are intertwined and defeat immediate review.

issues.label: Pendent merits review if jurisdiction is cured
preservationFacts: The contract interpretation issue was raised in summary judgment briefing.
recordSupportFacts: The supply agreement, purchase orders, and damages worksheet are in the lower-court record.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: If jurisdiction exists, the contract order misconstrued the termination clause.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Merits review should not occur unless appellate jurisdiction is first secure.

Use docketing statements to surface unresolved claims and possible Rule 54(b) cure paths.
Recognize when dismissal or a show-cause order is more realistic than merits review.

Notice of appeal references a nonfinal order.
Merits brief ignores pendent counterclaims that defeat appellate jurisdiction.

title: Preliminary Injunction Stay Appeal
shortCaption: Riverside Booksellers Ass'n v. City of Fairmont
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of West Virginia
proceduralPosture: District court denied a preliminary injunction against a city licensing ordinance, and appellant seeks emergency relief pending appeal.
issuesPresented: Whether appellant must seek a stay or injunction in the district court first.
Whether the preliminary injunction factors support emergency relief.
Whether expedited briefing is warranted.
meritsRecord: The ordinance requires event permits for sidewalk book displays within 500 feet of city hall.
The district court denied a preliminary injunction after finding no likely First Amendment violation.
Appellant filed a notice of appeal within fourteen days of the injunction order.
No district-court stay motion appears in the initial appellate record.
The next city festival is scheduled before ordinary briefing would conclude.

issues.label: District-court-first stay requirement
issues.standardOfReview: procedural prerequisite reviewed for abuse or practicality
preservationFacts: No stay motion was filed in the district court before the appellate emergency motion.
recordSupportFacts: The lower docket has no stay or injunction pending appeal entry.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: District-court-first practice should be excused because the festival date creates immediate harm.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The emergency motion should be denied or held until appellant seeks relief below.

issues.label: Preliminary injunction factors
issues.standardOfReview: abuse of discretion with legal conclusions reviewed de novo
preservationFacts: Likelihood of success, irreparable harm, equities, and public interest were argued below.
recordSupportFacts: Declarations from booksellers and city officials are available for appendix inclusion.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The ordinance burdens protected expression and imminent events establish irreparable harm.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The ordinance is a content-neutral time, place, and manner rule with available alternatives.

issues.label: Expedited briefing and emergency handling
preservationFacts: The notice and emergency motion identify a near-term event date.
recordSupportFacts: The city festival calendar and vendor notices are in the record.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: Expedited briefing is needed to prevent the appeal from becoming practically moot.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Expedition should not substitute for missing stay prerequisites.

learningObjectives: Prepare a stay pending appeal motion with district-court-first information.
Tie emergency motion metadata to the injunction factors and requested relief.
Use expedited briefing only after explaining why ordinary sequencing is inadequate.
modeledPitfalls: Emergency stay motion lacks district-court-first signal.
Relief requested is vague or not stated in motion metadata.
Expedition request substitutes urgency for likelihood-of-success analysis.

title: Qualified Immunity Interlocutory Appeal
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina
proceduralPosture: District court denied qualified immunity at summary judgment after finding disputed facts about a traffic-stop seizure.
issuesPresented: Whether interlocutory jurisdiction is limited to legal questions.
Whether the right was clearly established on the facts the district court assumed.
Whether the appellant impermissibly disputes the plaintiff's version of events.
meritsRecord: The district court identified a dispute over whether the plaintiff was handcuffed after complying.
The officer's body-camera footage is inconclusive after the first minute.
The district court denied qualified immunity on excessive-force and unlawful-seizure theories.
The notice of appeal invokes the collateral-order doctrine.
The opening brief challenges several of the district court's factual assumptions.

issues.label: Interlocutory jurisdiction over legal questions only
preservationFacts: The officer invoked qualified immunity in summary judgment briefing.
recordSupportFacts: The district court order separates assumed facts from legal conclusions.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: Even accepting the assumed facts, no clearly established law prohibited the conduct.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The appeal asks the court to revisit fact disputes and should be dismissed in part.

issues.label: Disputed fact framing
preservationFacts: The officer's summary judgment statement disputed plaintiff's account.
recordSupportFacts: Depositions and video exhibits conflict on the handcuffing sequence.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The video record permits review because no reasonable jury could accept plaintiff's account.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The appeal depends on factual disagreements that are outside interlocutory jurisdiction.

issues.label: Clearly established law
preservationFacts: The officer argued no materially similar authority existed.
recordSupportFacts: The parties cited Fourth Circuit excessive-force cases involving compliant detainees.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: Existing precedent did not clearly establish the alleged violation in the traffic-stop context.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The assumed facts fit clearly established excessive-force and seizure principles.

recordExcerpts.label: Qualified immunity denial order
recordExcerpts.text: The order denies qualified immunity after assuming plaintiff's account of compliance and handcuffing.

recordExcerpts.label: Body-camera exhibit summary

recordExcerpts.label: Plaintiff deposition excerpt
recordExcerpts.text: Plaintiff testified that he complied with commands before being pulled from the vehicle and handcuffed tightly.

recordExcerpts.label: Officer affidavit
recordExcerpts.text: The officer averred that plaintiff resisted and that any force was brief and proportionate.

recordExcerpts.label: Clearly established law chart
recordExcerpts.text: The parties collected Fourth Circuit authority concerning force against compliant or secured individuals.

learningObjectives: Separate appealable qualified-immunity legal questions from disputed facts.
Draft relief that respects the collateral-order posture.
Build an appendix that frames the district court's assumed facts clearly.
modeledPitfalls: Interlocutory jurisdiction limited to legal questions.
Opening brief contests facts rather than accepting the assumed record.
Requested relief seeks merits reversal beyond the court's jurisdiction.

The organization can address limits on fact-bound qualified-immunity appeals.

title: Post-Trial Contract JML Appeal
shortCaption: Blue Ridge Biologics, LLC v. Northstar Logistics Corp.
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia
proceduralPosture: After a jury verdict for Northstar, the district court denied renewed judgment as a matter of law and a new-trial motion.
issuesPresented: Whether Rule 50 arguments were preserved before submission to the jury.
Whether the district court abused its discretion in denying a new trial.
Whether damages evidence requires transcript excerpts and appendix support.
meritsRecord: Blue Ridge moved for judgment as a matter of law on causation but not on mitigation.
The jury returned a damages award that included storage costs and lost resale margin.
The renewed Rule 50 motion added a mitigation theory not raised before the verdict.
The new-trial motion argued the damages award was against the weight of the evidence.
The opening appendix lacks trial transcript excerpts for two key witnesses.

issues.label: Rule 50 preservation
preservationFacts: The preverdict Rule 50 motion addressed causation but not mitigation.
recordSupportFacts: Trial motion transcript excerpts show the exact grounds raised before the jury retired.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The preverdict motion fairly encompassed the renewed causation challenge.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The mitigation theory was not preserved and cannot support judgment as a matter of law.

issues.label: New-trial discretion
preservationFacts: The new-trial motion challenged the weight of the evidence and damages amount.
recordSupportFacts: Trial testimony and jury-instruction excerpts are required to evaluate discretion.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The damages verdict was against the clear weight of the evidence.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The district court reasonably deferred to the jury's credibility determinations.

issues.label: Damages record support
issues.standardOfReview: substantial evidence or abuse of discretion depending issue
preservationFacts: Damages were contested through trial testimony and post-trial briefing.
recordSupportFacts: The damages worksheet, expert testimony, and charge conference transcript are needed.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The award includes categories not supported by trial evidence.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The missing transcript excerpts require affirmance because appellant bears the record burden.

recordExcerpts.label: Damages worksheet

recordExcerpts.label: Transcript-order gap
recordExcerpts.text: The appellate docket contains no acknowledgment that the damages witness transcripts were ordered.

Match standards of review to Rule 50, new-trial, and damages challenges.
Build the appendix around trial motion and damages excerpts.

title: Sealed FOIA Record Appeal
shortCaption: Open Records Project v. Department of Energy
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland
proceduralPosture: District court granted summary judgment to the agency after reviewing sealed declarations and sample withheld records in camera.
issuesPresented: Whether sealed agency material must be handled through a sealed appendix and public redacted copy.
Whether the Vaughn index and agency declarations support the exemptions.
Whether public access and redaction obligations were satisfied.
meritsRecord: The agency withheld technical safety records under FOIA exemptions and filed classified-adjacent declarations under seal.
The district court reviewed sample records in camera and granted summary judgment.
The public docket contains a redacted declaration but the proposed appendix includes unredacted material.
The appellant challenges the adequacy of the Vaughn index.
No redaction acknowledgment accompanies the proposed sealed appendix.

issues.label: Sealed appendix and public redacted copy
issues.standardOfReview: procedural compliance reviewed for abuse of discretion
preservationFacts: The parties litigated sealing and redaction in the summary judgment record.
recordSupportFacts: The sealed declaration, public redacted declaration, and sealing order must be separated.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The appeal can proceed with sealed materials if a compliant public redacted copy is filed.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Unredacted sealed material cannot be filed publicly and should be rejected until corrected.

issues.label: Vaughn index and agency declaration adequacy
preservationFacts: The appellant challenged categorical declarations and segregability below.
recordSupportFacts: The Vaughn index and declaration excerpts are needed for merits review.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The index is too conclusory to permit meaningful review.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The declarations supply reasonably specific exemption and harm justifications.

issues.label: Public access and redaction obligations
issues.standardOfReview: abuse of discretion and de novo legal review
preservationFacts: The district court entered a sealing order and accepted public redactions.
recordSupportFacts: The public redacted declaration and sealing order are central record excerpts.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: Overbroad sealing obscures the basis for the judgment.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The sealed record protects sensitive technical details while public filings disclose enough for review.

recordExcerpts.label: Sealed agency declaration
recordExcerpts.text: The sealed declaration describes safety-sensitive systems and exemption harms in unredacted form.

recordExcerpts.label: Public redacted agency declaration
recordExcerpts.text: The public declaration redacts technical details but describes the exemption categories.

recordExcerpts.label: Vaughn index excerpt
recordExcerpts.text: The Vaughn index groups withheld records into categories and cites exemption rationales.

recordExcerpts.label: Sealing order
recordExcerpts.text: The district court permitted limited sealed filing with a public redacted copy requirement.

recordExcerpts.label: FOIA summary judgment opinion
recordExcerpts.text: The opinion grants summary judgment after relying on agency declarations and in camera review.

learningObjectives: Separate sealed, redacted, and public appendix materials in the filing workflow.
Use redaction acknowledgments and sealing metadata before submitting confidential material.
Argue FOIA record sufficiency without exposing sealed content in public filings.
modeledPitfalls: Sealed appendix filed without redaction acknowledgment.
Public copy omits enough context to support the FOIA arguments.
Brief cites sealed material without clear sealed-document metadata.

likelyAmici.interestStatement: The organization can address public access, redaction, and FOIA transparency principles.

title: Criminal Sentencing Appeal with Waiver
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina
proceduralPosture: Defendant filed a timely criminal notice of appeal after a within-Guidelines sentence; the government invokes an appellate waiver while defendant challenges Guidelines calculation and allocution.

participants.displayName: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina

issuesPresented: Whether the appellate waiver bars the Guidelines and reasonableness challenges.
Whether the district court plainly erred in applying a leadership enhancement.
Whether the court adequately considered allocution and mitigation under Section 3553(a).
meritsRecord: The plea agreement contains a waiver of appeal except for claims above the advisory Guidelines range or based on ineffective assistance.
The Rule 11 transcript includes a waiver colloquy but the court summarized the waiver in broad terms.
The presentence report recommended a two-level leadership enhancement based on disputed statements from co-defendants.
Defense counsel objected to the enhancement in writing but did not renew the objection after the court adopted the PSR.
The sentencing transcript shows a brief allocution and a within-Guidelines sentence of 84 months.

issues.label: Scope and validity of appellate waiver
issues.standardOfReview: de novo with plea-colloquy record review
preservationFacts: The government invokes the waiver in its response and appellee brief.
The Rule 11 transcript contains the district court's explanation of the waiver.
recordSupportFacts: The plea agreement and Rule 11 transcript are necessary to evaluate knowing and voluntary waiver.
The sentence fell within the advisory range adopted by the district court.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The waiver was not knowing because the colloquy described appeal rights too generally.
The allocution and procedural sentencing issues fall outside the waiver or satisfy miscarriage-of-justice limits.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The waiver is valid and bars ordinary Guidelines and reasonableness challenges.
The sentence was within the range covered by the agreement.

issues.label: Leadership enhancement at sentencing
issues.standardOfReview: clear error if preserved; plain error if forfeited
preservationFacts: Defense counsel filed a written objection to the PSR enhancement.
Counsel did not renew the objection after the court adopted the PSR findings.
recordSupportFacts: The PSR addendum and sentencing transcript identify the factual basis for the enhancement.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The record does not show control over another participant or organizing authority.
The written objection preserved the issue for ordinary sentencing review.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Co-defendant statements and drug ledger excerpts support the enhancement.
Any error is harmless because the sentence would be substantively reasonable.

issues.label: Allocution and mitigation explanation
issues.standardOfReview: abuse of discretion with procedural reasonableness review
preservationFacts: Defense counsel requested a variance based on family support and rehabilitation.
The defendant personally allocuted before sentence was imposed.
recordSupportFacts: The sentencing transcript includes the allocution and the court's explanation.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The court did not meaningfully address nonfrivolous mitigation arguments.
The explanation was too cursory to permit appellate review.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The court considered the parties' arguments and gave an adequate individualized explanation.
Any explanation error was harmless in light of the record.

recordExcerpts.label: Plea agreement appeal waiver
recordExcerpts.text: The plea agreement waives appeal of any sentence within or below the advisory Guidelines range, except for limited reserved claims.

recordExcerpts.label: Rule 11 waiver colloquy
recordExcerpts.text: The court asked whether Alvarez understood that he was giving up most appeal rights and confirmed counsel had reviewed the agreement.

recordExcerpts.label: PSR leadership enhancement excerpt
recordExcerpts.text: The PSR applies a two-level enhancement based on co-defendant statements that Alvarez directed deliveries and collected proceeds.

recordExcerpts.label: Sentencing transcript and allocution
recordExcerpts.text: Alvarez apologized, described rehabilitation efforts, and requested a variance before the court imposed an 84-month sentence.

recordExcerpts.label: Statement of reasons
recordExcerpts.text: The court adopted the PSR Guidelines range and cited deterrence, public safety, and Alvarez's history.

learningObjectives: Open a criminal appeal with the criminal notice event and required appearance materials.
Screen appeal-waiver issues before investing in ordinary sentencing merits briefing.
Build a sentencing appendix around the plea, Rule 11, PSR, and sentencing transcript excerpts.
modeledPitfalls: Opening brief ignores an enforceable appellate waiver.
Guidelines issue is argued without the PSR addendum or sentencing transcript.
Allocution challenge uses the wrong standard of review or omits harmless-error analysis.

title: Immigration Agency Review Petition
proceduralPosture: Petitioner seeks review of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision dismissing asylum and withholding claims and affirming denial of Convention Against Torture protection.

participants.displayName: Attorney General of the United States

issuesPresented: Whether the petition for review was timely from the Board's final order.
Whether the Board applied the correct nexus standard for family-based persecution.
Whether substantial evidence supports denial of Convention Against Torture protection.
meritsRecord: The Board dismissed the appeal thirty days before the petition for review was filed.
The immigration judge found credible testimony but concluded threats were motivated by generalized criminal extortion.
The Board adopted the immigration judge's nexus analysis and added a brief alternative finding.
Country-condition reports discuss police acquiescence in gang violence in the petitioner's home region.
The certified administrative record is incomplete because one translated declaration is missing from the index.

issues.label: Timely petition for review
preservationFacts: The petition for review was filed on the thirtieth day after the Board's final order.
The filing receipt and Board order date are both in the appellate record.
recordSupportFacts: The Board decision date and petition receipt establish the jurisdictional timeline.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The petition was filed within the statutory window measured from the final Board order.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Any defect in payment or service does not expand jurisdiction and must be checked at opening.

issues.label: Family-based persecution nexus
issues.standardOfReview: legal conclusions reviewed de novo; factual findings for substantial evidence
preservationFacts: The nexus argument was presented to the Board in the administrative appeal brief.
recordSupportFacts: The immigration judge's credible testimony finding and the Board's nexus paragraph are central excerpts.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The Board treated family membership as incidental despite targeted threats tied to the family relationship.
The Board's alternative finding did not cure the legal-standard error.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Substantial evidence supports the finding that criminal extortion, not protected status, motivated the threats.

issues.label: CAT acquiescence and country conditions
issues.standardOfReview: substantial evidence with de novo legal framing
preservationFacts: The CAT claim and police-acquiescence argument were exhausted before the Board.
recordSupportFacts: Country reports, declaration excerpts, and the immigration judge's CAT findings must appear in the agency record appendix.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The agency ignored material country-condition evidence of official acquiescence.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: The record does not compel a finding of likely torture with official acquiescence.

recordExcerpts.label: Board final order
recordExcerpts.text: The Board dismissed the appeal and adopted the immigration judge's nexus and CAT findings with a short supplemental explanation.

recordExcerpts.label: Petition for review receipt
recordExcerpts.text: The Fourth Circuit receipt shows the petition for review was filed on the thirtieth day after the Board order.

recordExcerpts.label: Immigration judge credibility finding
recordExcerpts.text: The immigration judge found Santos-Rivera credible but concluded the threats reflected generalized criminal extortion.

recordExcerpts.label: Country conditions report excerpt
recordExcerpts.text: The report describes repeated failures by local police to investigate gang threats in the petitioner's region.

recordExcerpts.label: Administrative record index gap
recordExcerpts.text: The certified index skips one translated declaration cited in the Board appeal brief.

learningObjectives: File a petition for review and docketing materials using agency-review event IDs.
Verify agency-review jurisdiction from the final order and petition receipt before briefing.
Use certified administrative record excerpts rather than district-court appendix assumptions.
modeledPitfalls: Petition for review filed under an ordinary notice-of-appeal event.
Brief cites missing administrative record material without a motion to supplement or correct.
Arguments collapse legal nexus review and substantial-evidence review into one standard.

likelyAmici.interestStatement: The organization can address recurring nexus and CAT evidence issues in petitions for review.

title: Original Mandamus Petition for Privileged Discovery
lowerTribunal: U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland
proceduralPosture: Corporate petitioner seeks mandamus after the district court ordered production of documents claimed to be attorney-client privileged and denied a stay pending review.

participants.displayName: U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland

issuesPresented: Whether mandamus is available to review a privileged discovery order before final judgment.
Whether petitioner lacks an adequate alternative remedy because production would destroy the privilege.
Whether emergency stay relief is warranted while the mandamus petition is screened.
meritsRecord: The district court ordered production of internal investigation memoranda within seven days.
The court found privilege waived by selective disclosure to outside auditors.
Petitioner moved for a stay in the district court, which was denied the same day.
The disputed documents have not yet been produced but the production deadline is imminent.
The privilege log and in camera index identify categories of memoranda and interview notes.

issues.label: Clear and indisputable right to writ relief
preservationFacts: Petitioner asserted privilege, requested in camera review, and sought a district-court stay.
recordSupportFacts: The discovery order, privilege log, and waiver ruling are necessary mandamus appendix materials.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: The order compels disclosure of core attorney-client communications based on an overbroad waiver theory.
Once produced, the privilege injury cannot be fully repaired on appeal from final judgment.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Mandamus is not a substitute for appeal and the waiver ruling is ordinary discovery management.
Petitioner has not shown a clear and indisputable right to relief.

issues.label: Adequate alternative remedy
preservationFacts: The district court denied stay relief before petitioner filed in the court of appeals.
recordSupportFacts: The stay denial and production deadline show why ordinary appeal may be inadequate.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: Post-judgment appeal cannot unring compelled disclosure of privileged memoranda.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Protective-order safeguards and final appeal provide adequate remedies.

issues.label: Emergency stay pending writ review
preservationFacts: Petitioner sought a stay first in the district court and attached the denial.
recordSupportFacts: The production deadline, stay denial, and privilege log support emergency relief.
likelyArgumentsForAppellant: A short administrative stay preserves the court's ability to consider the writ petition.
likelyArgumentsForAppellee: Emergency relief would delay discovery based on a weak privilege claim.

recordExcerpts.text: The district court ordered production of internal investigation memoranda within seven days after finding waiver.

recordExcerpts.label: Privilege log and in camera index
recordExcerpts.text: The privilege log lists attorney interview memoranda, compliance advice, and board presentation drafts.

recordExcerpts.label: District-court stay denial
recordExcerpts.text: The district court denied a stay pending mandamus and left the production deadline in place.

recordExcerpts.label: Auditor disclosure letter
recordExcerpts.text: The letter transmitted a high-level investigation summary to outside auditors without attaching attorney interview notes.

recordExcerpts.label: Protective order
recordExcerpts.text: The protective order limits use of produced material but does not claw back documents after intentional production.

learningObjectives: Open an original writ matter with a petition event rather than a notice of appeal.
Assemble a mandamus appendix that proves preservation, urgency, and lack of adequate remedy.
Pair emergency stay relief with a district-court-first record and a concrete production deadline.
modeledPitfalls: Writ petition filed as a direct appeal with the wrong initiating event.
Emergency motion omits the district-court stay denial.
Petition argues ordinary discovery error without clear-and-indisputable-right framing.

likelyAmici.interestStatement: The coalition can address privilege harms and mandamus treatment of compelled disclosure orders.
